body: Saturday, July 18 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: Fed Chair Warsh has publicly stated "prices are too high," and odds of a July rate hike have been rising per CNBC reporting. The 10Y yield sits at 4.54 (+8 bps vs 4W ago) and the 2Y at 4.18 (prior close, −2 bps), confirming the market is repricing the long end toward tighter conditions. The curve remains positively sloped at +37 bps — 8 bps steeper than four weeks ago but still flat by historical standards — consistent with a late-cycle economy tracking near Q1 pace. Fiscal dynamics remain expansionary — the deficit is "exploding" per Seeking Alpha — creating a structural tension between loose fiscal and a Fed that may need to tighten further.

New / Most Important: The June CPI slowdown weakened rate-hike expectations mid-week, but Warsh's hawkish rhetoric and the Iran/Hormuz energy supply shock have kept the hike scenario alive. The chip index fell into a bear market while the S&P 500 (7457, ↑0.5%) barely moved — a dangerous divergence showing extreme narrowing of leadership. Oil surging to 82.49 (↑7.4% vs 4W) is an inflationary impulse that directly complicates the Fed's calculus. Scott Bessent's comments about Fort Knox gold and the dollar's non-gold backing, alongside France pulling $15B in physical gold from US vaults, signal a new chapter in de-dollarization that is no longer theoretical but operational.

Playbook ✓: Economy holding up with stable labor market, strong earnings backstopping equities, VIX elevated but manageable at 18.77 — textbook "resilient but fragile" consensus.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The structural break is the simultaneous chip bear market and S&P near highs. This is NOT a healthy rotation — the Nasdaq 100 is down 3.6% vs 4W while the Russell 2000 is up 1.5%, a 5.3% relative swing. Capital is fleeing the AI-mega-cap complex and rotating into domestically-oriented small caps. This is what happens when the marginal dollar realizes that AI capex ($700B buildout per Warsh's colleagues) may fuel inflation rather than lower prices — the previous justification for paying infinite multiples on AI beneficiaries collapses. If this rotation persists, it marks the end of the concentration trade that has defined US equity markets for three years. The growth pulse confirms this is not a "risk-on" rotation but a defensive rebalancing wrapped in small-cap clothing: US single-family starts fell in June with building permits at a 10-month low, and China's household loans shrank by 366.8 billion yuan in the first half.

Macro Stance: The ECB is expected to hold rates at its next meeting but a September hike is now being discussed in Reuters polling, driven by energy price resurgence from Hormuz hostilities. The ECB itself has described the outlook as "extremely volatile." The UK economy is tracking materially stronger than expected, creating divergence within Europe.

New / Most Important: France physically pulled $15B in gold from US vaults — this is a seismic signal. It suggests a sovereign-level hedging decision against dollar-denominated reserve assets, and the feed indicates more European countries may follow. This is not a symbolic move; it is a capital flow event that redefines the transatlantic monetary relationship. Simultaneously, the ECB selected 36 payment service providers for the digital euro pilot, deliberately including previous critics — a smart political move to co-opt opposition. The Hormuz situation is existential for Europe's energy equation, directly feeding into the ECB's hawkish pivot discussion. SNB minutes showed inflation pressures "virtually unchanged" with monetary conditions deemed appropriate, suggesting Switzerland remains a relative haven of stability on the continent.

Playbook ✓: Energy-driven inflation complicating rate path is the consensus script playing out perfectly.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The gold repatriation is structurally new and breaks the post-Bretton Woods playbook. France moving physical gold out of the NY Fed's custody is the kind of action that historically precedes monetary regime changes. If Germany, the Netherlands, or Italy follow — and the feed suggests they might — this creates a feedback loop: reduced trust in dollar custody → reduced willingness to hold dollar reserves → structural dollar weakness. The digital euro pilot advancing simultaneously is not coincidental; Europe is building parallel monetary infrastructure. This is the most important cross-border capital flow signal in the feed.

Macro Stance: Policy rates are not the tool. A Reuters poll sees benchmark lending rates left unchanged for a 14th month in July ([Jul 17]), and the PBOC calls slower credit growth a "new normal" (Caixin, [Jul 16]) while easing through liquidity and a floor that bills not be re-discounted below 0.5% (Reuters, [Jul 14]). On the currency it sees a stable renminbi amid two-way fluctuations (China Daily, [Jul 16]), and the yuan weakened slightly as the PBOC lowered the daily fixing (BusinessToday Malaysia, [Jul 17]). Prices: June CPI rose 1% (Global Times, [Jul 9]) and producer inflation hit a four-year high (Reuters, [Jul 8]), cost-push that Bloomberg calls "bad inflation" ([Jul 15]).

PMIs & Activity: Second-quarter GDP grew 4.3%, below the official target range (Bloomberg, [Jul 15]), even as June industrial output rose 5.3% y/y and retail sales returned to growth (BusinessLine, [Jul 15]). The factory engine is AI- and export-led, with June exports up 27% y/y (Reuters, [Jul 13]) and the official manufacturing PMI at 50.3 (Reuters, [Jun 29]); Capital Economics calls AI the main driver of growth ([Jul 16]). Household demand is thin: Saucony saw a sharp slowdown in China retail growth in the second quarter while Anta and Fila managed low-single-digit gains (SGB Media, [Jul 17]), NEV retail sales fell 8% in the first two weeks of July (CnEVPost, [Jul 15]), and the WGC puts Chinese gold demand at a decade low in June (Mining.com, [Jul 17]).

Credit Impulse: This is the bottleneck. Household loans shrank by 366.8 billion yuan in the first half (36Kr, [Jul 17]), June credit growth missed forecasts (Caixin, [Jul 16]) and new bank loans rose less than expected (The Star, [Jul 15]), so the headline and the household book are both soft. Record consumer defaults undermine the push to boost spending (Reuters, [Jul 15]), and one of China's top investors argues finance, not AI, is the country's biggest bottleneck (CNBC, [Jul 16]). LGFVs that added debt face curbs on new bonds (Bloomberg, [Jul 15]), and foreign investors marginally offloaded onshore bonds in June (The Economic Times, [Jul 17]). The impulse is negative where it matters for consumption.

Property: Property investment slumped 18% y/y in January–June (The Standard, [Jul 15]). Price signals are confined to the top tier: China's top metros logged a fourth month of gains, lifting hopes of a housing recovery (Mingtiandi, [Jul 17]), while nationally new home prices declined at a slower pace (The Standard, [Jul 15]). Developers face a fresh liquidity crunch (Nikkei Asia, [Jul 13]), and shrinking household loans mean mortgage demand is not yet following the top-tier price turn.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Beijing eyes faster national infrastructure spending to steady growth amid a local investment slump (The Economic Times, [Jul 17]), in line with its bet on state-backed projects rather than broad stimulus (Reuters, [Jul 16]), and Caixin reports a rethink of the tax rebates that drove the export machine ([Jul 17]). The July Politburo meeting is being prepared (Sinocism, [Jul 13]). Europe is coordinating: Germany and France will draw up a roadmap on China trade imbalances (Bloomberg, [Jul 17]) by September (Le Monde, [Jul 17]) and vow to align on tougher measures (Financial Times, [Jul 17]). US signals are mixed: the Senate backed a 100% tariff bill on Russian oil buyers including China (The New Indian Express, [Jul 17]), while Washington lifted some Hong Kong sanctions (Reuters, [Jul 17]).

Markets & Flows: China stocks tumbled as CXMT's $8.6 billion IPO stirred liquidity concerns (TradingView, [Jul 17]) and faced steep weekly losses (The Economic Times, [Jul 17]); the Shanghai Composite breached 3,800 (BigGo Finance, [Jul 17]). The Hang Seng crashed over 2% in the tech sell-off (The Economic Times, [Jul 17]), with Z.ai sinking 28 percent (The Standard, [Jul 17]). Chinese AI also cut the other way abroad: the Nasdaq and S&P 500 dropped 1% after a Chinese AI breakthrough rattled tech stocks (CNN, [Jul 17]).

New / Most Important: The first-half household loan figure turns the "finance is the bottleneck" argument into data. Households are paying down 366.8 billion yuan of debt while the PBOC calls slower credit normal and keeps the loan prime rate on hold, so monetary easing has no transmission to consumption. Beijing's answer is faster infrastructure spending, which supports output and bulk demand but leaves the household balance sheet untouched. Rate cuts alone would not fix a credit-allocation problem; the Politburo meeting is where any shift toward household support would have to appear.

Playbook ✓: Household deleveraging, LPR on hold, investment-led support and a managed yuan are on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The consensus sees an infrastructure push as stimulus; the credit data say it is substitution, state borrowing replacing household borrowing. The transmission follows that split. Faster national projects are a modest support for iron ore and AUD after BHP won higher quarterly prices despite China's buying curbs (Reuters, [Jul 16]), but an 18% property-investment slump caps the upside. Consumer-facing exporters lose: weak household demand keeps hitting German carmakers, whose China sales plunged (AP News, [Jul 11]), just as Paris and Berlin align on tougher trade measures. Oil gains little while Chinese crude imports sit near a decade low (Bloomberg, [Jul 13]). For EM, ODI sees silver linings from China's slowdown for some economies ([Jul 17]), mainly through cheaper inputs rather than demand.

Macro Stance: The BOJ faces contradictory signals — the Takaichi government and the BOJ are sending conflicting messages that have rattled bond and currency markets. The yen is near multi-decade lows with USD/JPY eyeing 175 per forecasters, and intervention risk above 160 is growing. The BOJ paused bond-buying, leaving the yen further exposed.

New / Most Important: The structural crisis framing has intensified — "weak yen masks a structural crisis" is now the dominant narrative. MUFG sees a powerful long-term yen tailwind, but the near-term dynamics are ugly: the BOJ is trapped between defending the currency (requiring hikes) and protecting the JGB market (requiring accommodation). The bond-buying pause is a hawkish signal but markets are testing whether the BOJ has the conviction to follow through. Euro-yen has risen to the upper 185 range, meaning the yen is weak against everything, not just the dollar. Japanese firms themselves are flagging the weak yen as a bigger worry than BOJ hikes, which tells you the corporate sector is now net-hurt by depreciation — a structural shift from the old "weak yen helps exporters" playbook.

Playbook ✓: Yen weakness forcing BOJ's hand is consensus.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The government-BOJ contradiction is structurally dangerous. If the Takaichi administration is signaling it wants accommodation while the BOJ needs to hike, you get policy paralysis at the worst possible moment. Japan remains the global macro powder keg — a forced BOJ hike cycle unwinds the world's largest carry trade and sends shockwaves through global fixed income. The SCMP piece arguing Japan "can weather a US market crash" reads as consensus complacency given these structural fissures.

Macro Stance: The RBA is now facing rate hike pressure, reversing the prior easing consensus. Westpac has signaled a rate hike ahead, and multiple outlets report a fourth rate rise is more likely if the US-Iran conflict persists — energy pass-through is the transmission mechanism.

New / Most Important: This is a material hawkish repricing. Australia's economy is uniquely exposed: it imports energy price shocks via the Hormuz chokepoint while simultaneously facing a Chinese construction slump — property investment fell 18% y/y in January–June — that hurts its terms of trade, even as Beijing eyes faster infrastructure spending. The "big bank drops brutal forecast on homeowners" headline captures the household-level impact.  |  Playbook ✓: Energy-driven inflation forcing hawkish re-think is textbook.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The speed of this pivot from "all eyes on next cut" to "hike likely" is remarkable and reflects how fragile the global easing cycle narrative was. AUD is caught between commodity softness (bearish) and rate hike expectations (supportive) — a messy setup.

Macro Stance: The weekend summary from pb.pl is that Polish interest rates now "depend largely on the situation in the Middle East" ([Jul 18]), which is a fair reading of a week in which the NBP's hawks took the microphone. The bank disclosed who voted for a hike at an earlier meeting (Tysol.pl, [Jul 17]), a Council member said increases are more probable than cuts (Radio ESKA, [Jul 17]; pb.pl, [Jul 14]), and borrowers are being warned of higher instalments for many months (Direct Money, [Jul 17]). None of this is driven by current prices: June CPI was confirmed at 2.5% y/y with a 0.5% m/m fall (Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK, [Jul 15]), core inflation declined (Biznes Wprost, [Jul 16]) and food is cheapening at the fastest pace in years (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 16]). It is driven by what comes next: Eurostat's HICP already shows 3% y/y (Do Rzeczy, [Jul 17]), prices are rising faster than the EU average (Business Insider Polska, [Jul 17]), the expiry of the CPN fuel package will lift July inflation (Gazeta Prawna, [Jul 15]; Energetyka24.com, [Jul 16]) with PKO BP seeing a transitory move above 3.5% (PAP, [Jul 15]), and pb.pl reports experts no longer believe in post-holiday cuts ([Jul 15]).

Markets: Friday's close, now on the card, confirms the rotation out of banks: PKO 106.8 is -5.4% on the week and Pekao 229.0 -6.3%, leaving them +1.4% and -2.7% over four weeks, after Parkiet reported copper and geopolitics "sank KGHM and the banks" while Orlen and Żabka closed green ([Jul 17]). KGHM 293.7 is -4.9% on the week and -19.6% over four weeks following a 3.32% Friday drop (FXMAG, [Jul 17]), and a strong tremor at the Rudna mine injured two miners on Saturday (TVP Wrocław, [Jul 18]). The winners held: Orlen 146.2 (+4.5% 1W, +15.7% 4W), Allegro 43.4 (+9.0% / +10.1%) after its preliminary results (Inwestycje.pl, [Jul 14]), LPP 19960 (+3.0% / +7.5%), Dino 29.15 (+3.3%), PGE 9.48 (+1.2%), CD Projekt 232.2 (-0.3%). Żabka's 10.87% Friday jump on the Seven & i stake talks (FXMAG, Reuters, [Jul 17]) and Bankier's view that promotional prices on Allegro, Pepco and Żabka "are over" ([Jul 17]) describe a market Masłowski calls an advanced-phase bull run ([Jul 17]); INNPoland warns Żabka investing "is getting risky" ([Jul 17]). EPOL at 40.35 is flat on the week and +0.3% over four weeks, which is the whole Polish story in one number: record local index, flat dollar return. The zloty is the reason: EUR/PLN tested 4.35, the euro's highest since November 2024 (Interia Biznes, Business Insider Polska, [Jul 17]), with FXMAG reporting the zloty and Polish bonds "strongly down" ([Jul 17]); the card has USD/PLN 3.7782 (-0.2% 1W, +1.8% 4W) and EUR/PLN 4.328 (0.0% / +1.7%). The week's POLGB auction "again did not go as it should" (wnp.pl, [Jul 16]).

Fiscal & Politics: The half-year deficit of 123.7 billion zloty (Gazeta Prawna, [Jul 16]) framed everything: GlobEnergia costs the CPN package at 4.7 billion zloty for 92 days of relief ([Jul 17]), Domański quantified what presidential vetoes cost and said they weaken the economy's potential (TVN24, Wiadomości Onet, [Jul 17]), and public debt is 2.5 trillion zloty (wPolityce.pl, [Jul 14]). The policy response is heading toward the banks: Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK pushed back that "excess liquidity is not profit" and that further CIT increases would weaken lenders' ability to finance the economy ([Jul 18]), a direct reply to the proposed CIT hike (pb.pl, [Jul 14]). Energy politics escalated on Saturday: the president filed for a referendum on energy prices (wnp.pl, [Jul 18]) a day after the Sejm rejected his VAT cut on electricity (Bankier.pl, [Jul 17]), while the government published draft tariffs giving cheaper power to industry (Bankier.pl, Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 18]). Tax rates for 2027 are settled (wnp.pl, [Jul 17]).

Corporate & Sectors: Banks end the week with two open fronts. Nawrocki signed the CHF law allowing borrowers who sue to stop repaying, which Franknews expects to trigger a new wave of lawsuits ([Jul 18]; Next Gazeta.pl, [Jul 17]); the NBP had warned of exactly that (Parkiet, [Jul 14]). The benchmark reform has stalled, and the sector now wants the NBP reference rate written into mortgage law in place of WIBOR (Gazeta Prawna, [Jul 18]). Mortgage demand is still solid, with a record average loan and some banks lending over 1.3 million zloty (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 16]; Direct Money, [Jul 15]). Energy: Orlen adopted a biodiversity plan to 2030 (Energetyka24, [Jul 18]), the Sejm passed the Water Law amendment Orlen Termika sought (wnp.pl, [Jul 17]), and the nuclear plant on Pomerania is accelerating with a new rail link planned (Zawsze Pomorze, gwe24.pl, [Jul 18]). Retail: Dino's dispute with unions remains a scandal (INNPoland.pl, [Jul 17]) and Allegro and InPost are negotiating again (DlaHandlu.pl, [Jul 16]).

Geopolitics & Security: Fakt cautions against "overdoing the enthusiasm" about what Zelensky actually ordered regarding Poland ([Jul 18]), after a week in which support for helping Ukraine fell from 77% to 52% (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 16]) and attacks on Ukrainians in Poland drew warnings of more to come (Fakt, [Jul 16]). Washington detailed a new sanctions package on Russia (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 17]).

New / Most Important: The most important thing this week is a role reversal: the bank sector that carried WIG20 to records is now the policy shock absorber, facing a CIT increase, a signed CHF law and a stalled benchmark reform, while the NBP talks hikes on an oil shock the budget cannot afford to subsidise. A flat EPOL against a record WIG20 says international investors have already noticed. The referendum filing on energy prices adds a political layer to what was a fiscal problem.

Playbook ✓: Hold pattern with hawkish guidance into an oil shock is standard CEE central-bank behaviour; bank underperformance on tax and litigation risk is orthodox.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Inflation on target, core falling, yet the Council's public voices talk hikes and the zloty is at a post-2024 low: the market is pricing fiscal dominance, not price pressure. If the government reaches for bank CIT to close a 123.7 billion zloty gap, it taxes the sector that funds the deficit, and the auction stress already visible this week would be the first symptom.

Macro Stance: EM is bifurcated: oil importers face a stagflationary impulse from WTI at 82.49 (↑7.4%), while Russia's stock market is described as "raddled." Vietnam's Vietcombank chairman acknowledged domestic savings are insufficient to support GDP growth above 10%, explicitly flagging the need for foreign capital inflows — a structurally honest admission.  |  New / Most Important: The EM ETF that "beat the S&P 500 for 16 years" headline reflects renewed interest in EM as a diversification play amid US tech sell-off. Vietnam's capital gap framing is investable intelligence — it tells you exactly what policy concessions Hanoi will need to make to attract FDI.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Rising oil prices typically crush EM net importers (India, Turkey), but if the energy shock is paired with dollar weakness from gold repatriation dynamics, the EM complex could surprise to the upside.

Narrative: The Nasdaq 100 is down 3.6% vs 4W ago, the worst major index, after a broad AI sell-off that put the chip index in a bear market; Apple near all-time highs is the odd one out, and the "Magnificent Seven bubble" debate is now mainstream.

Reported: IBM's stock plunged 25% after its Q2 earnings miss (TIKR.com, [Jul 15]), its worst crash of all time (Fortune, [Jul 15]), and the inside story of the warning still dominates (WSJ, [Jul 17]). Wipro lagged peers after an earnings miss and a weak forecast (Reuters, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: Cloudflare — analysts are raising AI and security targets (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 16]), as security budgets hold up while legacy software is squeezed.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Warsh's colleagues warning that the $700B AI buildout will "fuel persistent inflation" inverts the bull case: if AI capex is inflationary rather than deflationary, the driver of tech revenue is also what keeps the Fed hawkish, a reflexive trap no prior tech cycle faced.
Narrative: Google and Tesla loom large in next week's earnings, leaving the sector caught between AI excitement around Google and the broader tech sell-off.

Reported: Netflix's forecast disappointed and the shares tumbled (Reuters, [Jul 17]), with Wall Street cutting targets on weak guidance (CNBC, [Jul 17]). Publicis raised its guidance on new business wins (WSJ, [Jul 16]), while Telenor cut guidance for the second time in two quarters (Telecoms, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: Alphabet — earnings are expected to grow ahead of next week's release (Yahoo Finance Australia, [Jul 15]), with Google Cloud growth, TPU sales and Gemini in focus (IG, [Jul 15]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The World Cup is proving a winner for Bell Media's digital strategy (The Globe and Mail, [Jul 17]) while Netflix stumbles: this summer the ad growth sits with live sports, not with on-demand libraries.

Narrative: A steeper curve (+37 bps, 8 bps steeper than four weeks ago but still flat by historical standards) is modestly positive for bank NIMs, and Russell 2000 outperformance (↑1.5%) usually comes with regional-bank strength.

Reported: Truist beat with EPS up 37% (Quartz, [Jul 17]), and Travelers beat on lower catastrophe losses (The Globe and Mail, [Jul 17]). Danske Bank raised its profit outlook on Nordic-wide growth (Reuters, [Jul 17]), and U.S. Bancorp posted record quarterly revenue on loan growth (Reuters, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: Robinhood — Goldman Sachs raised its target ahead of earnings (TheStreet, [Jul 17]), riding the record trading activity the big banks just reported.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Deutsche Bank is flagged as exposed to inflation and geopolitical risk, the canary for European bank stress if the ECB is forced to hike into a supply shock, even as Nordic peers raise their outlooks.

Narrative: WTI at 82.49 (↑7.4% vs 4W) on the Iran/Hormuz escalation, even after OPEC output jumped 3.05M bpd in June. The bid is supply, not demand: China's second-quarter growth slowed to 4.3% and its crude imports sit near a decade low.

Reported: BP sees a boost from energy prices in the second quarter but flags a $1 billion impairment (Reuters, [Jul 14]). Oil companies are making billions, and US calls to tax the windfall are growing (NPR, [Jul 16]).

EPS Upside Watch: European majors — European earnings growth is seen at its strongest in 3 years as energy profits surge (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 16]). US producers — oil and gas employment is at a 2026 low even as production sets records, so operating leverage is at a cycle high.

⚡ Breaking Convention: A Hormuz supply shock, record US output and falling energy employment at once mean the sector has de-risked its cost base: higher prices no longer feed the usual wage loop, making XLE more leveraged to price and a cleaner geopolitical hedge than in 2022.

Narrative: Transportation stocks fuelled the rally this week, small-cap outperformance (Russell ↑1.5%) and breadth favour domestically oriented industrials, and the space economy (UBS sees a $1.3T market by 2040) adds a growth layer.

Reported: GE Aerospace beat and lifted guidance on services growth (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 16]). Cintas jumped 7% on a beat and a Bank of America upgrade (TIKR.com, [Jul 17]). ABB beat Q2 forecasts and announced a $5.5B Rotork acquisition (Global Banking & Finance Review, [Jul 16]).
EPS Upside Watch: Insteel Industries — a re-rating supported by an improving earnings outlook (Seeking Alpha, [Jul 17]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The space premium is more speculative than the TAM suggests: SpaceX has shed over $1T of market value since mid-June after a scrubbed Starship launch, and its shares tumbled again on an aborted launch (Moomoo, [Jul 17]).
Narrative: Tesla's earnings loom next week, and JPMorgan's study showing Gen Z prioritises vacation savings over retirement suggests spending on experiences is structural, not cyclical.

Reported: Richemont's sales beat lifted the luxury sector as jewellery shines (Reuters, [Jul 15]). Frasers Group grew revenue and retail profits as international expansion accelerates (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 16]). Reliance Retail's Q1 net profit fell 14.1% despite higher revenue (Business Standard, [Jul 17]).
EPS Upside Watch: Amazon — a Q2 preview sees a massive advantage in powering the AI race (Seeking Alpha, [Jul 17]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Experience spending may be structural, but it is price-led: Olive Garden's rare $100 deal sparked a massive customer rush (TheStreet, [Jul 17]). Traffic follows discounts, which caps restaurant margins even when demand holds.

Narrative: Defensive rotation is under way with the VIX elevated at 18.77 (↑1.8%), and Warsh's "prices are too high" framing keeps consumer price sensitivity front of mind, favouring staples with pricing power.

Reported: Conagra fell as guidance disappointed and it cut its dividend (Barron's, [Jul 15]), alongside a $2 billion charge (MarketWatch, [Jul 15]). PepsiCo's turnaround stutters as Americans rethink snacking (Reuters, [Jul 14]).
EPS Upside Watch: Walmart — another move to win higher-income shoppers (TheStreet, [Jul 14]) supports mix and margins.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The defensive bid is not reaching packaged food: the US grocery slowdown is deepening as shoppers buy fewer items, raising pressure on food companies (CNBC, [Jul 16]). Pricing power is narrower than the sector label implies.
Narrative: Healthcare benefits from the defensive rotation but lacks a sector-wide catalyst, so results are judged stock by stock.

Reported: UnitedHealth blew past estimates and hiked its earnings outlook as it reins in costs (CNBC, [Jul 16]). Abbott raised its 2026 profit forecast on strength in diagnostics and medical devices (Reuters, [Jul 16]). Intuitive Surgical tumbled 11% despite topping expectations (TIKR.com, [Jul 17]).
EPS Upside Watch: Humana — earnings estimates are rising (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 16]) as managed-care cost trends improve.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Coverage, not cost, is the new risk: Intuitive ties its Q2 procedure softness to ACA subsidy expirations (MedTech Dive, [Jul 17]) after HCA cut on coverage losses (Healthcare Dive, [Jul 14]). Volume risk is reaching a sector assumed to be immune.

Narrative: Copper at 6.22 (↓4.0% vs 4W) trades as an AI data-centre and grid-capex metal and is sliding with the chip bear market. The cyclical read comes from China's credit and property data: household loans shrank by 366.8 billion yuan in the first half and property investment fell 18% y/y in January–June.

Reported: Alcoa cut its aluminum production guidance (Barchart.com, [Jul 17]). BASF lifted guidance as higher chemical prices boost earnings (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 15]). Higher sales volumes and prices drove significant earnings increases at Valterra (Mining Weekly, [Jul 17]).
EPS Upside Watch: Itaconix — raised its 2026 revenue guidance after record first-half sales growth (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 17]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Gold at 4012, down 7.9% while tensions escalate and sovereigns repatriate physical gold, is a genuine anomaly: with BTC outrunning gold by 15.8 points over 4W, a physical-paper divergence is building that historically resolves violently upward.
Narrative: Rising 10Y yields (4.54, +8 bps) are a headwind; mortgage rates are easing slightly, but the direction of the long end matters more for REIT valuations.

Reported: Prologis raised guidance after a record quarter for leasing (Estates Gazette, [Jul 16]). UK housebuilder Crest Nicholson sank to a loss amid a 'challenging' housing market (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 16]). Oberoi Realty's Q1 profit rose 29% but missed estimates (Business Standard, [Jul 17]).
EPS Upside Watch: None flagged.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Prices say otherwise than the rate story: Cohen & Steers reports amid a REIT market rally (Investing.com UK, [Jul 16]), and AEW UK REIT is weighing a counter bid for Alternative Income REIT (QuotedData, [Jul 16]). Buyers are paying for property the bearish consensus marks down.
Narrative: AI data-centre power demand remains a secular tailwind, but rising yields compress the rate-sensitive premium; the tension between the two defines the sector.
Reported: No major reports this week.
EPS Upside Watch: AI-power utilities — screens are picking names built for the coming AI power crunch (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 17]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: If AI capex is inflationary by the Fed's own assessment, utilities are both the beneficiary (power demand) and the victim (higher rates) of the same phenomenon, a structurally ambiguous setup that argues against a clean bond-proxy or growth label.
Narrative: Rising energy costs from the Hormuz tensions pressure European manufacturing margins, and ECB hike risk compounds the headwind through tighter consumer credit.

Reported: Volvo Cars flagged weak profitability in a challenging China market (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 17]) but sees a stronger second half despite rising costs (Reuters, [Jul 17]). Supplier Autoliv beat Q2 estimates on Asia growth and cost savings (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 17]).
EPS Upside Watch: None flagged.
